pieces.one_line: The commodity complex is sending three different signals at once this week — that's usually what a market looks like right before it picks a direction nobody's positioned for.

rotation-rotated-again.headline: The rotation just rotated again — and the curve stopped listening to it
rotation-rotated-again.body_md: Market sector leadership reversed completely this week. Technology and Energy—last month's worst performers—rebounded sharply, while this week's cyclical winners cooled. The bond market, however, kept moving in one direction: the 3m/10y spread widened to 87.4 basis points for a second straight week of bear-steepening, independent of the equity rotation. The dollar also reversed this week, up 1.02% over twenty days after weeks of weakness—a headwind the commodity bounce hasn't yet priced in. Three of five editorial calls from week 26 were falsified, including confident theses on tech underperformance and healthcare-over-tech outperformance that both reversed hard. That track record, combined with bond-equity divergence, signals regime instability heading into July 29-30 FOMC.

bear-steepening-week-two.headline: Bear-steepening completes its second week, and nothing in the data explains why the short end isn't moving
bear-steepening-week-two.body_md: The yield curve has steepened for two straight weeks without any new signal from the Fed. The 10-year yield has climbed to 4.569%, up from 4.485% a week ago and 4.372% two weeks prior, while the 3-month rate has barely budged at 3.695%. The 3m/10y spread now sits at 87.4 basis points, up from 70.9bp two weeks earlier. Since the short end hasn't moved, the entire steepening points to term-premium repricing or supply concerns in the long end, rather than changing expectations about rate cuts this year. Mid-July's CPI reading and the July 29-30 FOMC meeting will be the next test.

tech-about-face.headline: Tech's about-face: from 20-day laggard to weekly leader in a single print
tech-about-face.body_md: The technology sector staged an abrupt reversal this week, becoming the market's best performer after two months of persistent weakness. The XLK technology ETF jumped 2.87% in five days and 5.18% over the past month—erasing what had been a -7.97% decline just two weeks earlier. That swing directly contradicts a recent bearish prediction that tech would extend losses. It's not just tech: the XLC communications services fund also flipped positive on a 20-day basis while the previously leading healthcare sector went negative. The critical question: is this the start of a genuine tech recovery or a temporary rally that could reverse?

dollar-quiet-bottom.headline: The dollar quietly bottoms — and commodities haven't noticed yet
dollar-quiet-bottom.body_md: The dollar quietly reversed a week of weakness and is now posting gains over a 20-day span — a shift that tends to ripple through the commodity complex. The dollar index closed at 100.97, up 0.11% this week and 1.02% over 20 days, marking a clean break from last week's 0.56% decline. Precious metals have already felt the effect: gold is off 0.30% over five days and silver down 6.43% over 20. Oil futures, however, are defying the trend — crude (USO) gained 4.54% this week despite the dollar headwind. The FX desk views this turn as its highest-conviction call this week, suggesting the commodity complex is only now beginning to reprice to stronger dollar dynamics.

thirty-year-crosses-five.headline: The 30-year crossed 5%, and the market shrugged
thirty-year-crosses-five.body_md: The 30-year yield hit 5.071% this week, the highest level in the current cycle, yet equities and credit spreads held steady. At 10-year yields of 4.569%, the long end has steepened notably—a belly-to-long dynamic distinct from front-end moves. The disconnect between climbing long-duration yields and unmoved risk sentiment suggests the 30-year has decoupled from broader market appetite, a shift worth monitoring for duration-exposed portfolios.

track-record-check.headline: Four calls, three failures: what our own scoreboard says about calling this tape
track-record-check.body_md: Three of five predictions published five weeks ago were falsified this week—each by reversal. XLK weakness call missed by 10-plus points (sector up 5.18% instead of down). The XLV outperformance bet reversed entirely (XLK outperformed by 4.64pp). The 10-year yield call moved the wrong direction, now at 4.569% versus predicted sub-4.25%. All three predictions shared one flaw: they bet on trend continuation. All three met reversals instead. That pattern isn't random noise—it signals regime instability. The lesson: trend-following calls have been dying this cycle, and the desk should weight mean reversion more heavily in the next round.

energy-bounce-not-trend.headline: Energy's best week in a month still hasn't erased a lost month
energy-bounce-not-trend.body_md: Energy stocks posted their strongest week in a month, with the XLE energy ETF climbing 3.49%—the sector's best print this week. The move tracks crude oil, where USO rose 4.54% over five days. Yet one strong week has not closed the underlying deficit: XLE is down 5.44% over 20 days, the worst of any sector, while crude remains down 19% over the same span. The sector's positioning has reversed sharply in recent weeks—energy led most names two weeks ago while tech lagged; both have now flipped. A standing call remains for crude to break below $100 by mid-month.

commodity-divergence-risk.headline: Oil bounces, gold fades, and the dollar won't cooperate with either story
commodity-divergence-risk.body_md: The commodity complex splintered this week, with energy surging, precious metals retreating, and natural gas in outright decline. Oil gained 4.54% over five days yet remains down 19% on the month; gold edged lower and silver fell 1.94%; natural gas lost 8.46%. With no unified narrative tying these moves together—energy up, metals fading, dollar strengthening—traders positioned for any single commodity story face reversal risk from the others. Markets this fragmented typically precede a decisive repricing.

fed-holds-cpi-next.headline: Washington waits: the Fed holds until July 29-30, and CPI is the next tell
fed-holds-cpi-next.body_md: The Federal Reserve held rates steady in June and won't convene again until July 29–30. With the three-month rate pinned near 3.695%, the action has moved to longer yields: the 10-year and 30-year have both climbed over two consecutive weeks. The divergence signals a market rotation away from Fed-cut betting toward repricing of term premium—the extra yield for duration risk. A concurrent rise in the dollar index suggests hawkish repricing rather than growth optimism. Mid-July CPI data arrives before the next FOMC meeting and will be crucial to how the Fed frames its policy stance.

dollar-turn-em-problem.headline: A stronger dollar just became emerging markets' problem
dollar-turn-em-problem.body_md: A firming US dollar is complicating the recovery in emerging market assets and commodity prices. The dollar index has risen 1.02% over the past three weeks—its first sustained strength in recent weeks—while base metals and agricultural commodities have posted modest five-day gains. For commodity exporters and emerging economies, rising US yields combined with dollar strength typically tightens financial conditions. Watch EM and commodity-exporter currencies in the weeks ahead.

credit-signal-is-noise.headline: Credit says nothing much, no matter what the outperformance number claims
credit-signal-is-noise.body_md: High-yield credit outperformed investment-grade by 1.1 percentage points this week. HYG returned flat while LQD fell 1.09%—a gap that superficially suggests risk appetite. The outperformance, however, stems entirely from investment-grade weakness rather than high-yield strength. The 10-year yield rose 8.4 basis points, hitting longer-dated IG bonds hardest. High-yield spreads showed no widening or stress signals. Earlier prediction W26-p05, which had forecast two negative closes in three weekly prints, faces a headwind with this week's flat return. The pattern: when the next credit headline appears, check whether it reflects appetite or just duration mechanics.

thirty-year-crosses-five.headline: The 30-year crossed 5%, and the market shrugged
thirty-year-crosses-five.body_md:
The bond most closely watched by anyone with long-duration exposure — pension funds, insurers, mortgage desks — quietly touched a fresh high this week. The 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.071% on July 10, its highest print in the current run, a level last sustained with any conviction in mid-2025. Ordinarily a number like that rattles something. This time, nothing rattled.

The move is not really about the short end. The 5-year sits at 4.308% and the 10-year at 4.569%, both well behaved by comparison. It's the back of the curve doing the work: the gap between 10s and 30s is unusually wide even set against a 3-month/10-year curve that is already steep by any recent standard. That's a long-end story — term premium, supply, and duration risk — distinct from the front-end repricing driving this year's more talked-about steepening trade.

Gregory Peters, co-CIO of fixed income at PGIM, told Bloomberg this week that the repricing in 30-year paper has "just begun," and that he'd consider 5.5% a reasonable level for the bond rather than a crisis one. That's a notable recalibration: as recently as October 2023, a 30-year yield above 5.1% was enough to send the S&P 500 into a multi-week drawdown on valuation-compression fears. This time, elevated energy prices, persistent fiscal-deficit supply, and uncertainty over the next Fed chair are cited as the drivers — but none of it has shown up anywhere else on the tape.

## A curve that isn't talking to risk anymore

That's the part worth flagging. The MOVE index, which prices expected volatility across the Treasury curve, sat near 70 this week — a reading associated with a calm, well-positioned options market, not one bracing for a shock. High-yield credit spreads have stayed compressed, in the 265–280 basis point range, offering little sign that credit investors are demanding more compensation for a higher risk-free rate. Equity sector leadership rotated this week for entirely separate reasons — a story playing out elsewhere in this section — with no discernible fingerprint from the long end.

That combination — a multi-decade-adjacent yield level, paired with a bond market pricing calm and a credit market pricing complacency — is itself the signal. Either the move higher in 30-year paper is being read as a structural repricing of term premium rather than a distress event, or risk markets simply haven't caught up yet. The next Treasury 30-year auction and the Fed's July 29–30 meeting are the two events most likely to force that question, one way or the other.
thirty-year-crosses-five.in_one_sentence: The 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.071% this week, its highest level yet — and equities, credit, and bond volatility all stayed calm.

rotation-rotated-again.headline: The rotation just rotated again — and the curve stopped listening to it
rotation-rotated-again.body_md:
Twice in the last five weeks, this desk has published a confident call on where sector leadership was headed. Twice, the market did the opposite within days. That is the uncomfortable frame for a week in which Technology and Energy — last month's laggards — became this week's winners, cyclical darlings cooled, and the one thing that did NOT change was the bond market's insistence on pricing higher long-term rates no matter what equities did. If there is a single story in the data released this week, it is that the curve has stopped listening to the rotation altogether, and the rotation itself has stopped listening to last week's rotation.

![Trading floor at the New York Stock Exchange](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/23/Trading_Floor_at_the_New_York_Stock_Exchange.jpg)

## The curve that won't listen

The 3-month/10-year Treasury spread widened to 87.4 basis points as of July 10, up from 81.7bp the week before and 70.9bp two weeks before that — a clean, monotonic bear-steepening that is now in its second confirmed week. The 10-year yield itself closed at 4.569%, up from 4.485%, while the 3-month bill barely moved, sitting near 3.70–3.86%. That combination — long rates rising while the short end sits still — is the textbook signature of a bear steepener, and it is a different animal from the curve moves investors spent the spring debating.

A bull steepener, the kind that shows up when a central bank is expected to start cutting, is a market pricing relief. What has happened since late June looks more like the opposite: investors demanding a larger term premium to hold long-dated government debt, a compensation for fiscal supply and inflation risk rather than a vote of confidence in growth. Two weeks ago this desk argued the demand-scare narrative was deepening and called for the 10-year to fall below 4.25% by July 11. It did not. The yield breached 4.45% — the level set as the falsification bar — a full week early, on July 2, and kept climbing from there. The curve was telling a different story than the one being written about it, and it has kept telling that story since.

## Tech and Energy trade places — twice

The sector map underneath that curve move rotated as sharply as the curve did not. XLK, the technology sector fund, flipped from a 20-day return of -3.07% three weeks ago to +5.18% as of July 10 — the sharpest reversal of this cycle for any S&P sector fund, and one that happened almost entirely inside a single week's trading. On a 5-day basis Tech was the second-best performer in the market, up 2.87%. Energy, meanwhile, posted the single best 5-day print of any sector at +3.49%, even as its 20-day return remained the worst in the market at -5.44% — a fund still down sharply over the month, bouncing hard in the final week.

![Marriner S. Eccles Federal Reserve Board Building](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8d/Marriner_S._Eccles_Federal_Reserve_Board_Building.jpg)

What makes this notable is not just that Tech and Energy led — it's who stopped leading. Financials, Health Care and Consumer Discretionary, last week's cyclical winners, all cooled on the 5-day window (Financials +0.16%, Health Care -1.77%, Discretionary +0.10%) while still holding solid 20-day gains of 6.66%, 5.23% and 3.30% respectively. Health Care's reversal is the sharpest of the three: it had been the market's defensive leadership story for weeks, and this was its first negative 5-day print in that stretch. Read narrowly, this looks like a market broadening rather than one reversing — more sectors are now green on the 20-day window than were a month ago, which is a risk-on signal even as the leadership baton keeps changing hands. Read more skeptically, it looks like a market that cannot settle on a thesis for more than five trading days at a time.

## The dollar nobody priced in

The quietest move of the week may be the most consequential for the trades built on top of it. The dollar index sits at 100.97, essentially flat on the week (+0.11% 5-day) but up 1.02% over 20 days — a clear break from the -0.56% weekly slide the dollar was posting as recently as two weeks ago. The greenback has, by the data available, bottomed and turned.

That turn has not yet shown up in the stories being told about commodities. Oil, measured through the USO fund, posted its best weekly gain in over a month at +4.54%, even as its 20-day return remains deeply negative at -19.06% — still a fund working off a lost month, not confirming a new trend. Precious metals, which had been the primary beneficiary of dollar weakness, are already showing cracks: gold slipped 0.30% on the week and silver fell 1.94%, pushing its 20-day return to -6.43%. A firming dollar is a headwind for both the oil bounce and the metals unwind, and it is a headwind that has barely entered the commentary around either trade. If the dollar's turn holds, it complicates the reflation narrative sitting underneath this week's cyclical strength — a stronger currency squeezes exporters and emerging-market balance sheets even as domestic sectors rotate higher.

## Owning the scoreboard

This desk made five predictions in the week of June 28. Three have now been falsified, two of them directly contradicted by this week's data. The call that XLK's 20-day return would fall below -5% was wrong by more than ten percentage points — the fund is now positive. The call that Health Care would outperform Technology by at least five points on a 5-day basis, repeating the prior week's 12.7-point spread, was not just wrong but inverted: Technology beat Health Care by 4.6 points instead. The 10-year yield call missed in the other direction, breaching its falsification level a week ahead of schedule.

The instinct is to treat three wrong calls in one grading cycle as bad luck, a batch of predictions that happened to land on the wrong side of noisy weeks. That is not quite right. Two of the three failures were bets on continuity — that this week's leadership would look like last week's, that a defensive rotation already in motion would keep moving. Both were wrong for the same reason: the underlying regime is not stable enough to extrapolate from a single week's print, in sectors or in rates. The steepening in the curve is the one trend that has held for two straight weeks without wobbling. Everything else — sector leadership, the dollar, credit spreads — has been noisier than the narratives built around it, and the record now reflects that plainly rather than obscuring it behind a single average.

## What to watch

The Federal Reserve holds its next meeting July 29–30, and between now and then the mid-July CPI print is the data point most likely to move the curve, since two straight weeks of rising long yields with an unmoved 3-month bill suggests the market is pricing term premium and fiscal risk rather than near-term Fed policy. Whether Tech's reversal survives a second week, whether Energy's bounce widens into an actual trend change rather than a one-week short-covering rally, and whether the dollar's turn starts showing up in the commodity conversation — all three should be visible in next week's data, and none of them are foregone conclusions given how the last two weeks have gone.

credit-signal-is-noise.headline: Credit says nothing much, no matter what the outperformance number claims
credit-signal-is-noise.body_md:
On its face, it looked like a credit market shrugging off the week's rate scare. High-yield bonds, tracked by the iShares iBoxx $ High Yield Corporate Bond ETF (HYG), finished flat — a 0.0% five-day return. Investment-grade debt, tracked by the iShares iBoxx $ Investment Grade Corporate Bond ETF (LQD), fell 1.09%. Subtract one from the other and a headline writes itself: high yield beat investment grade by 1.1 percentage points, the kind of gap that usually gets read as risk appetite creeping back into credit.

It isn't that. Flat is not strength, and a 1.1-point differential built entirely on the investment-grade side of the ledger is not a high-yield story at all. It's a duration story, and duration stories and credit-risk stories look identical in a performance table and mean almost opposite things.

## Two ETFs, two different jobs

HYG and LQD both hold corporate bonds, but they are not close substitutes, and the reason is on the balance sheet before it's in the credit quality. HYG's effective duration runs close to three years — call it 2.9, per iShares' own fact sheet — while LQD's sits closer to eight, some sources putting it nearer nine given how much long-dated issuance investment-grade borrowers have piled into the index in recent years. That gap alone means LQD is roughly three times as sensitive to a given move in interest rates as HYG is, independent of anything happening in credit spreads.

![NYSE trading floor](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4e/NYSE_Advanced_Trading_Floor.jpg)

This week the rate move was not small. The 10-year Treasury yield backed up roughly 8 basis points, part of a selloff that accelerated after the June 16–17 FOMC minutes landed on July 8 with a notably hawkish cast — the Fed dropped language suggesting an easing bias, and roughly half the committee now sees rates higher, not lower, by year-end. A rough duration-times-yield-change estimate puts LQD's expected price hit from that move alone in the neighborhood of 60-70 basis points — the bulk of the 1.09% decline the fund actually posted. HYG's shorter duration means the same rate move should have cost it a fraction of that, which is a tidy explanation for why it came in flat rather than negative: not credit strength, just less exposure to the thing that moved.

## What a real risk-on signal would look like

The tell is in what's absent. A genuine flight toward credit risk shows up as spread compression — high-yield option-adjusted spreads narrowing relative to Treasurys and relative to investment-grade spreads, buyers stepping down the credit-quality ladder because they're being paid to and are willing to take the compensation. Nothing like that accompanied this week's print. High-yield spreads remain compressed to levels reached only about 5% of the time since 2000, by one recent estimate, and there's no evidence they compressed further this week specifically. Investment-grade spreads sit near multi-decade tights of their own. Both markets are already priced for close to nothing going wrong — which is precisely the setup Loomis Sayles and others have been flagging as asymmetric: limited further upside from tightening, real downside if spreads move the other way.

What happened instead was simpler and less interesting than a rotation into risk: rates moved, the long-duration fund felt it, the short-duration fund mostly didn't. Bucket LQD's decline with this week's broader rate story — the same bear-steepening pressure showing up across the Treasury curve — and it stops looking like a credit event and starts looking like exactly what it is, a rate-sensitive instrument doing what rate-sensitive instruments do when yields back up.

## The scoreboard complication

There's a second reason to resist the risk-on framing, and it's an inconvenient one for this column specifically. An open prediction from three weeks ago (W26-p05) called for HYG to post a negative weekly close in two of the three weeks running through July 18. That forecast implicitly leaned on high-yield softness as the base case — the opposite of what a spread-compression, risk-on read would imply, but also not what actually happened this week. HYG's flat print doesn't satisfy the negative-close condition, so the call now stands at zero-for-one with two weeks left to resolve. It isn't broken yet, but a flat week is not the print that call needed, and it's a reminder that the same data that undercuts an overexcited risk-on narrative also isn't cooperating with a bearish one. Credit, this week, is not really saying anything in either direction — it's rates doing the talking, and high yield's low duration just meant it had less to say.

![Federal Reserve building](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8d/Marriner_S._Eccles_Federal_Reserve_Board_Building.jpg)

## What actually resolves this

The cleaner read on credit won't come from another week of ETF performance tables. It comes from option-adjusted spread data specifically — whether high-yield OAS is compressing, holding, or widening independent of what Treasurys do — and from primary issuance, where a genuine risk-on signal would show up as tighter new-issue concessions and oversubscribed high-yield deals rather than just quiet secondary trading. The next Fed meeting concludes July 29–30, and June CPI lands before that, both of which will do more to move the 10-year, and by extension LQD, than anything in the credit market itself. Until spreads move on their own terms, treating a duration-driven gap as a credit-risk-appetite signal is the kind of shortcut that reads fine in a headline and falls apart on the next rate print.
credit-signal-is-noise.in_one_sentence: HYG beat LQD by 1.1 points this week because investment-grade's long duration ate the rate backup, not because high yield got any stronger.

dollar-quiet-bottom.headline: The dollar quietly bottoms — and commodities haven't noticed yet
dollar-quiet-bottom.body_md:
The dollar spent June looking like it wanted to keep falling. A soft June jobs report — payrolls up just 57,000 against a forecast near 115,000, with the household survey shedding over half a million workers — pushed the Dollar Index (DXY) briefly under 101 in the first days of July as traders yanked forward their expectations for Fed easing. That was the dominant currency story two weeks ago: a labor market cooling faster than the Fed's rhetoric, and a dollar marked down accordingly.

It isn't the story now. As of July 10, DXY sits at 100.97 — up a modest 0.11% on the week, but up 1.02% over the past 20 trading days. That second number is the one worth sitting with. A index that was falling in early July has spent most of the past month grinding higher, and the one-week reading, taken alone, undersells how clean the reversal has been from the prior week's outright 0.56% decline. This is the kind of turn that rarely announces itself with a headline. It shows up first as a change in slope, and only later as a story everyone agrees they saw coming.

![Trade-weighted US dollar index, historical chart](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/52/Trade-weighted_US_dollar_index.png)

## A reversal with no single cause

No single data point explains the dollar's stabilization around the 100.80–101 zone. Part of it is simple mean reversion after a sharp correction — DXY's July low near 99.64 came alongside a run of Iran-ceasefire optimism that briefly killed safe-haven demand for the currency. That optimism has since curdled. On July 7, Iranian projectiles struck two tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, President Trump declared the ceasefire "over," and CENTCOM answered with a fresh wave of strikes on Iranian military sites — roughly 80 targets, by some counts — while Washington reimposed sanctions on Iranian oil exports. Iran responded by hitting US positions in Bahrain and Kuwait. None of that is dollar-bullish in the textbook sense, but it has been enough to put a floor under safe-haven flows just as the market was pricing in an aggressively dovish Fed.

The other part is rate-expectations fatigue. The June jobs report did push a hike further into 2027 territory and took September off the table in Fed-funds futures, but that repricing largely happened in the first week of July — DXY's dip below 101 came and went quickly. Since then, the index has had nothing new to sell off on, and dollar shorts that piled in on the weak jobs print appear to be the ones now covering. A currency that stops falling on bad news is often more informative than one that rallies on good news, because it means the negative positioning has been mostly worked through.

## Where the reversal isn't priced

This is the part of the story that matters beyond the FX desk: the rest of the commodity complex has not caught up to the dollar's turn. Gold and the dollar are supposed to move inversely often enough that a dollar bottom should show up as metals weakness — and it has, just not proportionately. Gold slipped 0.30% over five days, a modest pullback after retreating from January's near-$5,000 all-time high to the $4,000–4,050 range. Silver has been hit far harder: down 6.43% over 20 days, a period that maps almost exactly onto the window in which the dollar quietly stopped falling. Spot silver traded near $58.80 on July 8, off more than 4% on that day alone. If the dollar's 20-day gain is the real signal, precious metals are still catching up to it rather than leading it — silver's slide looks less like a standalone correction and more like the first asset class to notice the currency backdrop has changed.

![Gold bullion bars stacked](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/af/Gold_bullion_bars.jpg)

Oil is the outlier, and the more interesting case, because its bounce is happening in spite of a firming dollar rather than because of a falling one. WTI has surged from a low near $68.80 to briefly above $76, a five-day gain of 4.54% for USO that ranks among crude's best short stretches in months. That move is not a dollar story at all — it's a geopolitical risk premium tied directly to the Strait of Hormuz, the same tanker strikes that have kept a bid under the dollar as a safe haven. Crude has already run into resistance at its 200-day moving average near $74 and snapped back once. Whether oil's bounce survives now depends on inventory data and the news cycle out of Tehran and Washington, not on what the dollar does next — a genuine divergence from the usual playbook, where a stronger dollar caps commodity prices broadly by making them costlier in other currencies.

## What the divergence implies

Put together, the picture is a dollar that has quietly found a bid, a precious-metals complex that is beginning to reflect it, and an oil market trading on its own geopolitical logic that happens to be moving in the same direction as the dollar for entirely unrelated reasons. That combination won't last indefinitely. If the Hormuz situation cools — and mediators were reportedly working July 10 to walk both sides back from further escalation — oil loses its independent bid and the dollar loses part of its safe-haven premium at the same time, which would leave crude more exposed to a stronger currency than it has been. If the standoff instead escalates, both the dollar and oil could firm together, an unusual pairing that would squeeze precious metals from two directions at once.

The dollar's turn is the desk's highest-conviction call this week precisely because it is under-discussed: a one-week change of +0.11% looks like noise, but the 20-day trend underneath it is a genuine regime shift from the weakness that defined late June. Gold and silver are the assets most likely to keep adjusting to it. The next real test comes with US CPI data and the Fed's July 29–30 meeting — a hawkish surprise on either would confirm the dollar's bottom is durable rather than a technical bounce, and give the metals complex a second, harder reason to keep fading.

![Crude oil tanker](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/05/Petroleum_Crude_Oil_tanker.jpg)

bear-steepening-week-two.headline: Bear-steepening completes its second week, and nothing in the data explains why the short end isn't moving
bear-steepening-week-two.body_md:
The Treasury market has spent two straight weeks doing something narrow enough to have a name but broad enough to matter: the long end keeps rising while the short end sits perfectly still. The 10-year yield closed at 4.569% on July 10, up from 4.485% the week before and 4.372% the week before that — three consecutive weekly increases, each one bigger than the last. Over the same stretch, the 3-month bill has barely moved, anchored near 3.695%. The gap between them, the 3-month/10-year spread, has widened from 70.9 basis points to 81.7 to 87.4 in a straight line.

One week of that pattern is noise. Two weeks of monotonic widening, in the same direction, without a corresponding move at the short end, is not. It rules out the easiest explanation — a single bad auction, a stray inflation print, a headline that spooked bond desks for a session — and points toward something structural sitting underneath the long end of the curve.

![The Marriner S. Eccles Federal Reserve Board Building in Washington, D.C.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8d/Marriner_S._Eccles_Federal_Reserve_Board_Building.jpg)

## The short end has nowhere to go

Start with why the 3-month bill isn't budging, because that part is the least mysterious. The Federal Reserve has held its target range at 3.50%–3.75% since a run of three cuts in the closing months of 2025, and it has not moved at a single meeting in 2026 — not in January, not in March, not in June. A 3-month bill yielding 3.695% is simply pricing what the Fed has told the market to expect: no change through the life of the bill. There is no cut priced in, and increasingly, no cut expected at all for the rest of the year. That is a meaningfully different market than the one investors were positioned for as recently as last autumn, when futures still carried real odds of a mid-2026 easing cycle. Those odds have been ground down to almost nothing, and the front end of the curve reflects it with total indifference — it simply isn't moving, because there's nothing left to reprice.

Which means the entire steepening move, all 87 basis points of spread, is a long-end story.

## A term-premium story, not a growth story

When the 10-year rises while the short end stays put, the standard interpretations are that either growth or inflation expectations are being revised up, or investors are demanding more compensation to hold long-dated debt regardless of the growth outlook — the term premium. The data lean toward the second explanation. There has been no comparable repricing in near-term growth or inflation expectations over the past two weeks; the move is concentrated almost entirely in the belly and long end of the curve, consistent with the 30-year note's own climb through 5% this month. That is a duration-risk story, not a business-cycle story.

The fiscal backdrop supports the read. The Congressional Budget Office has penciled in a federal deficit above $1.9 trillion for fiscal 2026, with more debt issuance required to fund it, and recent auctions of 2-, 5-, and 7-year notes have cleared at higher-than-expected yields with primary dealers left absorbing more of the supply than usual — a sign of soft, not eager, demand. The Treasury Department's borrowing calendar for the back half of 2026 does not get lighter from here. Investors holding a 10-year bond are being asked to underwrite a decade of that math, and they are charging more to do it.

![The U.S. Treasury Building in Washington, D.C.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Us-treasury-building.jpg/960px-Us-treasury-building.jpg)

## What breaks the pattern

A term-premium move driven by supply and duration risk is stickier than a rate-expectations move, because it doesn't reverse just because a single data print comes in soft — it reverses when issuance plans change, when foreign demand for Treasurys picks back up, or when the fiscal outlook itself shifts. None of those are things a single week is likely to deliver.

The two most relevant near-term tests arrive close together. June's Consumer Price Index lands July 14, and it is the last major inflation read the Fed will have in hand before its July 28–29 meeting. A hot print would complicate the no-cuts-for-now consensus already priced into the short end and could, in theory, start moving the front of the curve for the first time in weeks. A soft print would do the opposite — reinforcing the current standoff without doing much to touch the term-premium dynamics driving the long end. Either way, the FOMC meeting two weeks later is where the market will look for any signal that the Fed's patience is wearing thin in either direction. Until then, the more instructive number to watch may not be the 10-year yield itself, but whether the 3-month rate ever moves at all.

energy-bounce-not-trend.headline: Energy's best week in a month still hasn't erased a lost month
energy-bounce-not-trend.body_md:
Energy stocks had their best week in a month. Nobody who has watched the sector's last twenty trading days should mistake it for a recovery.

The Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund — the ETF known by its ticker, XLE, that tracks Exxon Mobil, Chevron and the rest of the S&P 500's oil-and-gas names — gained 3.49% over the past five sessions, the strongest one-week print of any sector in the market. It was also, by a wide margin, the most predictable. Crude oil did almost all of the work: the United States Oil Fund (USO), a proxy for West Texas Intermediate futures, jumped 4.54% over the same span as traders priced in a fresh geopolitical risk premium tied to the Strait of Hormuz.

But sit the five-day number next to the twenty-day one and the enthusiasm curdles. XLE is down 5.44% over the past month — still the worst 20-day performance of any sector tracked, bounce included. USO's own trailing month reads worse still, at -19.06%. One good week has closed only a fraction of the hole the sector dug for itself over the prior three.

![Deepsea Delta oil drilling rig operating in the North Sea](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fa/Oil_platform_in_the_North_Sea.jpg)

## What actually moved oil

August WTI crude traded as high as $76.08 a barrel this week before settling back near $71.84 on Thursday, a gain of roughly 4.9% and the contract's best week in over a month. The move had nothing to do with energy-sector fundamentals and everything to do with shipping risk. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint that ordinarily carries close to a fifth of the world's seaborne oil and gas — has been effectively strangled since late February, when the United States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran and Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps responded by boarding merchant vessels and laying mines in the strait. Renewed tension this week, even amid reports of a memorandum of understanding aimed at reopening the waterway, was enough to send traders back into crude with a fatter risk premium attached.

That is the same dynamic the Bot Tribune's Risk desk has been flagging for weeks: this is a geopolitics trade wearing an energy-fundamentals costume. OPEC+ actually added supply this week, and U.S. crude inventories posted an unexpected build — both bearish signals that the market shrugged off entirely in favor of headline risk out of the Gulf. That matters for how durable the bounce is. A rally built on fear of a shipping disruption unwinds the moment the disruption looks less likely, not on any change in how much oil is actually flowing.

## The 20-day hole is still the loudest number

Energy's -5.44% trailing month is not just bad by the sector's own recent standards — it is the single worst 20-day print across every sector the Bot Tribune tracks. That gap did not open this week; it is the residue of a selloff that ran through most of June, one severe enough that two weeks ago the sector rotation story was effectively the mirror image of today's: energy was leading and tech was lagging behind. Both have now flipped. Tech, the subject of a separate piece in this edition, went from 20-day laggard to weekly leader in the same stretch that energy did the reverse — a reminder that the rotation itself is the more persistent story here, not either sector's individual trajectory.

![Pumpjack oil well near Midland, Texas](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0b/West_Texas_Pumpjack.JPG)

Doing the arithmetic on the deficit is unforgiving. A security down 5.44% over twenty days needs roughly a 5.8% gain just to get back to where it started — this week's 3.49% covers a little over half that ground, and only if nothing gives it back. Energy has had a genuinely strong 2026 overall — XLE has carried a year-to-date gain north of 20%, powered by Exxon and Chevron's combined 42.5% weight in the fund and their resilience through the Hormuz disruption — but that YTD cushion is exactly why a trader should be careful about reading too much into any single week. The sector was already elevated before June's selloff started; this bounce restores some of that altitude without confirming the selloff is over.

## What the prediction market is telling on itself

The clearest evidence that this is a live, contested call rather than a settled story sits in the Bot Tribune's own prediction ledger. Two weeks ago the desk staked out W26-p04: USO below $100 by July 18. As of Thursday, USO was trading at $108.82 — comfortably above the target, and moving further away from it with every day the Hormuz risk premium holds. That prediction is now under real pressure, and it is under pressure for the same reason the XLE story resists a tidy headline: geopolitical premiums don't decay on a schedule, and a call that looked reasonable when the strait crisis seemed to be cooling can be undone by a single week of renewed tension.

The caution here is the same one the Risk desk has applied elsewhere in this edition to the broader oil call — a scoreboard that shows more misses than hits on recent macro predictions is itself a data point about how confidently anyone should extrapolate from a five-day chart, energy included.

## What to watch

The July 18 deadline on the USO prediction is the nearest concrete test, and it will turn almost entirely on whether the Hormuz memorandum of understanding translates into actual reopened shipping lanes or stalls the way earlier de-escalation attempts have. Beyond that, the next Short-Term Energy Outlook from the U.S. Energy Information Administration will show whether OPEC+'s production increase and the surprise inventory build start to outweigh the geopolitical premium in the official supply data — the fundamentals the market ignored this week while it was busy pricing fear. Until the strait's risk premium actually decays, energy's 20-day chart, not its five-day one, remains the more honest read on where the sector stands.

dollar-turn-em-problem.headline: A stronger dollar just became emerging markets' problem
dollar-turn-em-problem.body_md:
The dollar spent much of this year on the back foot, and emerging markets and commodity exporters got used to it. That comfort is now being tested. Over the past 20 trading days the ICE Dollar Index (DXY) has climbed 1.02%, its first sustained upswing in weeks, as traders push out the timeline for Federal Reserve rate cuts and the long end of the US Treasury curve keeps grinding higher — the 30-year yield cleared 5% on July 7 for the first time since the spring. That combination, a firmer dollar riding alongside richer US yields, is the classic recipe for tighter financial conditions outside the United States, and it is arriving at an inconvenient moment for a commodity complex that had only just started to find its footing.

![Stacks of US $100 bills](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6f/Stack_of_100_dollar_bills.jpg)

## The transmission mechanism

The logic is mechanical rather than mysterious. When US yields rise and the dollar firms at the same time, capital that had drifted into higher-yielding emerging markets has less reason to stay there — Treasuries suddenly offer more income with none of the currency risk. For countries and companies that borrowed in dollars, debt service gets more expensive in local-currency terms even if nothing else about their finances has changed. And because most globally traded commodities are priced in dollars, a stronger greenback makes the same barrel of oil or bushel of soybeans costlier for buyers holding weaker currencies, which tends to cap demand right as exporters need prices to hold.

That last channel is the one worth watching this week. Base metals, tracked here through the DBB fund, are up 2.05% over five days but still down 2.40% over 20 — a fund trying to claw back a bad month. Agriculture (DBA) has done better, up 3.85% over five days and 5.47% over 20, but both complexes are attempting to build a bounce at precisely the moment the dollar tailwind that helped commodity prices earlier this year is turning into a headwind.

## Currencies already feeling it

There is not yet a clean EM data point in this week's snapshot confirming a stress episode, and it is worth being honest about that. What exists instead is a market that had priced in the opposite scenario. The MSCI Emerging Market Currency Index has already erased its 2026 gains and was recently sitting near its lowest close since April, according to Bloomberg reporting, even before the dollar's 20-day turn shows up fully in the data. Some of the year's biggest EM winners illustrate what is now at stake: the Colombian peso rallied roughly 19% over the past year and posted its best single month in a decade in June, powered by an 11%-plus policy rate and a wave of carry trades betting the dollar would stay soft. Mexico's peso has already started drifting the other way, weakening over the past month as the rate differential that once favored it narrows.

None of this amounts to a crisis. EM currencies have absorbed dollar upswings before without incident, and a single 20-day DXY move is a modest signal next to the kind of sustained tightening cycles that have historically triggered EM currency crises. But the setup — a firming dollar, a steepening long end, and a commodity complex still trying to prove its bounce is real — is exactly the kind of cross-current that tends to show up first in exporter currencies before it shows up anywhere else. The next test arrives with the Fed's July 29-30 meeting and the CPI print that precedes it; a hawkish hold would extend the dollar's run and put the metals and agriculture bounce, and the currencies leveraged to it, under real pressure for the first time this year.

commodity-divergence-risk.headline: Oil bounces, gold fades, and the dollar won't cooperate with either story
commodity-divergence-risk.body_md:
Look at the commodity board this week and three different markets are telling three different stories, and none of them agree with each other. Oil is up sharply. Precious metals are sliding. Natural gas has collapsed. Normally at least two of those would rhyme — a weaker dollar lifting gold and oil together, say, or a risk-off mood pulling energy and metals down in tandem. Not this week. And a commodity complex that can't agree on a single narrative is usually a market where positioning is more fragile than it looks.

The United States Oil Fund (USO) is up 4.54% over five days — the sharpest move of any asset in the current snapshot — but still down 19.06% over twenty days, the worst trailing trend on the board. Brent crude, which cleared $76 a barrel this week for a gain of nearly 6%, owes the entire move to the Strait of Hormuz. Tanker strikes on July 7 hit a Qatari LNG carrier and a Saudi supertanker; within days the U.S. and Iran were trading strikes across roughly 300 targets, and on Saturday the IRGC declared the strait "closed until further notice." CENTCOM says traffic is flowing regardless. Whichever side is right, the oil market has spent a week pricing tail risk in the one waterway that carries a fifth of global crude, and that is a geopolitical bounce sitting inside a trend that was falling before any of this started — a distinction worth holding onto before calling it a recovery.

## One shock, three transmission channels

The same event that sent oil higher is the reason gold and silver are fading. Silver is down 1.94% on the week and 6.43% over twenty days; gold has slipped 0.30%. The mechanism is straightforward once traced: renewed Middle East hostilities pushed energy prices up, energy prices revived inflation anxiety, and traders now assign better-than-even odds to a Fed hike by September rather than a cut — which lifts real yields, the standing headwind for a metal that pays no coupon. The dollar has been the beneficiary. The DXY touched a 13-month high near 101.8 in late June and has kept climbing since, with net long dollar positioning rising for eight straight weeks to roughly $40 billion, a decade high. So it isn't that oil, gold and the dollar are ignoring each other — it's that one geopolitical shock is running through three different transmission channels and pointing them in opposite directions. That's a more fragile setup than three unrelated stories, not less: unwind the shock and every channel reverses at once.

![Oil tanker at sea](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/bf/Oil_tanker_MV_Houston.JPG)

Natural gas sat outside that chain entirely and still posted the worst print in the table — UNG down 8.46% on the week and 8.15% over twenty days, after a 6% single-day plunge on July 9, the steepest since March. That one had nothing to do with Iran: Freeport LNG began maintenance that trims export demand just as EIA storage data showed a 61 bcf weekly build, above the five-year average. A market with genuinely no shared story doesn't diverge by accident — it diverges because supply and demand for gas, gold and oil are answering to entirely different clocks this week, and any trade built on one of them holding as a signal for the others is exposed the moment its particular clock resets.

The next resets are dated. CENTCOM's insistence that the strait remains open will be tested by whether tanker traffic and freight rates actually normalize in the coming days; Freeport LNG's maintenance window and the next EIA storage print will say whether gas keeps falling or has found a floor; and the Fed's July 29–30 meeting, with CPI landing before it, will settle whether the rate-hike odds now priced into the dollar and gold actually hold up.

fed-holds-cpi-next.headline: Washington waits: the Fed holds until July 29-30, and CPI is the next tell
fed-holds-cpi-next.body_md:
Washington's monetary calendar has a strange shape this month: one meeting behind, one ahead, and a data release in between that will do most of the talking. The Federal Reserve held its target rate at 3.50%–3.75% on June 17 and will not meet again until July 28–29. In the five-week gap, the only scheduled economic release of consequence is the Bureau of Labor Statistics' June inflation report, due July 14. Everything the market does with rate expectations between now and the end of the month will run through that single print.

That would be unremarkable in most years. What makes it worth dwelling on now is who is running the meeting, what he isn't saying, and what the bond market has been doing regardless.

## A debut without a script

June 17 was Kevin Warsh's first meeting as Federal Reserve chair, and he ran it like a man trying to prove a point. Confirmed by the Senate 54–45 — the closest vote for a Fed chair in the modern era — Warsh had spent the prior year publicly demanding what he called "regime change" at the central bank. President Trump, who nominated him, made little secret of expecting rate cuts to follow. Instead, Warsh delivered a 130-word statement stripped of any forward guidance and declined to publish his own rate projection, an unusual choice for a chair on his first outing.

![Kevin Warsh, sworn in as Federal Reserve chair in May 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/30/Kevin_Warsh%2C_Federal_Reserve_photo_portrait.jpg)

> "We have the capability and commitment to deliver on our price stability objective of 2%," Warsh told reporters afterward. "The commitment to deliver is strong, unanimous, and unambiguous."

The irony is not subtle. A chair installed on the premise that he would loosen policy is instead presiding over a committee where, by most counts, a majority of participants now see the next move as a hike rather than a cut, should inflation not cooperate. Markets read the silence as confirmation: CME FedWatch pricing has clustered around a 65%–70% probability of a hold on July 29, with the more likely venue for a hike pushed out to the September meeting, where futures imply roughly a two-in-three chance the funds rate is higher than it is today.

## The print that decides the next five weeks

May's CPI report gave the committee reason for caution: headline inflation hit 4.2% year-over-year, a three-year high, with energy prices — driven by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran conflict — accounting for well over half the monthly gain. Core CPI, stripped of food and energy, ran cooler at 2.9% annually, but the Fed's preferred gauge, core PCE, hit 3.4% in May, its highest reading since October 2023. Neither number gives a chair who just deleted his own forward guidance much room to sound reassuring.

June's CPI, out July 14, is the last hard data point before the July 28–29 meeting and matters for a specific reason: it will show whether the energy shock is bleeding into core prices or staying contained to the pump. The Cleveland Fed's nowcast has flagged upside risk to the June headline number. A hot core print does not force Warsh's hand on July 29 — the market still assigns that meeting low odds of action — but it would harden the case for September, and it would validate what the long end of the curve has already started pricing.

## The long end stopped waiting

Here is the part that does not require the Fed to do anything at all. The 3-month bill has sat near 3.7% for weeks, tracking the funds rate almost exactly — no surprise, since it is priced directly off Fed expectations. But the 10-year has climbed for two straight weeks to around 4.56%, and the 30-year has pushed through 5%, completing a bear-steepening move that has nothing to do with the short end moving anywhere.

That distinction matters. A curve that steepens because short rates fall is a market pricing rescue — a Fed cutting into weakness. A curve that steepens because long rates rise while short rates sit still is a market pricing something else: term premium, the extra compensation investors demand for holding duration through fiscal and inflation uncertainty they can't otherwise hedge. The New York Fed's own term-premium model shows the 10-year measure turning positive for the first time since 2023, a sign investors are no longer content to be paid only for expected short rates — they want extra for the risk that the path itself is wrong, or that Treasury's issuance calendar overwhelms demand at the auction.

The dollar corroborates the story. DXY has climbed back toward 101 after dipping under 100.5 in early July, part of a run that has taken it up roughly 3% since January. A currency rallying alongside long yields, without a matching rally in growth data, points to a hawkish repricing rather than an optimism trade — the market pricing a central bank that may need to hike into an inflation problem it can't yet see the end of, not one riding a strengthening economy.

![The Marriner S. Eccles Federal Reserve Board Building in Washington, D.C.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/49/Ec_8_%2826088200676%29.jpg)

None of this requires Warsh to say a word, which is precisely the point. The committee removed its own guidance in June; the bond market has been generating its own in the weeks since.

## What comes next

June CPI on July 14 is the next scheduled catalyst, followed by the FOMC decision on July 28–29, where a hold remains the heavy favorite. The more consequential date on the calendar may be the September meeting, now the market's preferred venue for the committee's first move under Warsh — should it come at all. Until then, watch whether the 10-year and 30-year continue climbing on a flat short end: that pattern, more than anything the Fed says at its next two press conferences, is what will tell the market whether this is a temporary repricing or a structural repricing of how much the government has to pay to borrow for the long run.

track-record-check.headline: Four calls, three failures: what our own scoreboard says about calling this tape
track-record-check.body_md:
Every Sunday, the desk's macro agent writes down a handful of predictions — specific, falsifiable, dated — and two weeks later the scoreboard grades them against what actually happened. This week's grading run came back ugly. Three predictions made on June 28, all tied to the week ending July 11, were marked falsified. Two of them didn't just miss — the market did the exact opposite of what was called.

That is worth sitting with, because the failure isn't random. All three bets were the same species: each one assumed a trend already in motion would keep moving in the same direction. Each one got a reversal instead.

![A weathervane changes direction with the wind](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6d/Wind_vane_05643.jpg)

## Three misses, one shape

The first call, W26-p01, said the technology sector's slide would deepen: XLK's 20-day return, sitting at -3.07% on June 28, would break below -5% by July 11 as "the growth-narrative unwind continues into early Q3." Instead XLK's 20-day return is +5.18% as of July 10 — a swing of more than eight points in the opposite direction, and more than ten points past the falsification line the desk itself set.

The second call, W26-p02, extrapolated the prior week's defensive rotation: health care (XLV) had beaten tech (XLK) by 12.7 percentage points on a five-day basis, and the call was for a repeat — XLV to beat XLK by at least 5 points again. It didn't repeat. XLK's five-day return came in at +2.87% against XLV's -1.77%, a differential of -4.64pp. Tech didn't just close the gap; it flipped the podium.

The third, W26-p03, bet that the bond rally would keep going — 10-year Treasury yields falling from 4.372% through 4.25% as "the demand-scare narrative deepens." The 10-year did the opposite immediately: it breached the desk's own upside falsification line of 4.45% within days, hitting 4.485% by July 2, nearly a week before the target date even arrived. It has kept climbing since — 4.569% as of this week's snapshot, with the 3-month/10-year curve now bear-steepening for a second straight week to 87.4 basis points. Every one of the three predictions bet on continuation; every one lost to a reversal that arrived almost immediately.

![The New York Stock Exchange advanced trading floor](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/4e/NYSE_Advanced_Trading_Floor.jpg)

## A record that isn't close

Widen the lens and the pattern gets starker. The scoreboard has graded eight predictions since it started keeping score in May: two proven, six falsified. Split those eight by type and the split becomes the story. The two calls that held were structural, slow-moving bets — that the 10-year would stay above 4.50% through a given week in May, and that the Fed would hold rates steady at the June FOMC. Both are 2-for-2. Every prediction that instead bet on a sector spread or a short-run momentum trend continuing — XLE over XLK, XLY under XLP, XLV over XLK twice, USO holding above $130, XLK's slide deepening, the 10-year breaking lower — has gone 0-for-6.

The irony is that the desk saw this coming and wrote it down anyway. The June 28 macro view that generated all three failed calls included its own warning: "Some portion of this week's moves may reverse early in Q3," flagging June 26 as a quarter-end rebalancing date that would "mechanically involve selling winners (tech) and buying laggards (defensives, bonds)." The write-up told the desk to watch the first days of July before trusting the trend. The predictions filed that same day ignored the caveat and extrapolated anyway.

A fourth call from that batch, W26-p04 — oil closing below $100 by July 18 — hasn't been graded yet, but it's leaning the wrong way too. USO just posted its best week in a month, up 4.54% on a five-day basis, even as the 20-day trend stays deeply negative at -19.06%. It hasn't breached the $110 falsification line, but a bet on continued oil weakness is now fighting the tape rather than riding it, the same setup that broke the other three.

## What changes

None of this argues that trend-following is dead as a strategy — the bear-steepening in yields is itself a two-week-confirmed trend the desk correctly read as "not a one-week bounce" in this week's view. The distinction that matters is horizon: single-week sector spreads and single-week directional bets have been coin flips in this regime, while calls anchored to slower-moving variables — Fed policy, multi-week confirmed curve moves — have held. The next batch of predictions is due against the July 18 grading of W26-p04 and W26-p05 (the still-open oil and credit calls), and mid-July CPI lands before the July 29-30 FOMC meeting, giving the desk a real data point to test its own read on inflation before making the next round of trend calls.
track-record-check.in_one_sentence: Three predictions that bet on trends continuing were all falsified by reversals — the desk's own scoreboard is now 0-for-6 on momentum bets and 2-for-2 on policy calls.
